summary: Registers the MIME subtype audio/32KADPCM, for toll quality audio using 32 kbit/s ADPCM as defined in ITU-T G.726. It obsoletes RFC 2422.

plainLanguage.summary: This gives a name tag for a certain phone-quality sound format so mail can carry it.

questions: what is g.726 adpcm in mime
how are adpcm code words packed into bytes
subtitle: Registers the MIME type that carries 32 kbit/s ADPCM telephone-quality voice, with a fixed bit order.

tldr.problem: Voice messaging over Internet mail needs a registered MIME type for 32 kbit/s ADPCM audio, and implementations of G.726 disagree on the order of the four-bit code words in a byte.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers audio/32KADPCM, which holds raw G.726 data with no header and permits only little endian packing of code words.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2422 with only editorial and boilerplate changes, and also obsoletes the earlier registration in RFC 1911.

today: RFC 3802 is a Draft Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaced RFC 2422.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3802 registers the MIME sub-type audio/32KADPCM for toll quality audio. The encoding itself is defined by the ITU-T in Recommendation G.726. The RFC obsoletes an earlier sub-type registration in RFC 1911 and also obsoletes RFC 2422.

A section titled Changes from RFC 2422 states that only editorial and boilerplate changes were made.
sections.plainLanguage: This note gives an official name to one kind of phone-quality sound so email programs know what it is.

sections.title: The ITU-T Definition
sections.content:
Recommendation G.726 defines the recommended conversion of a 64 kbit/s A-law or mu-law pulse code modulation (PCM) channel at 8000 samples/second to and from a 40, 32, 24 or 16 kbit/s channel. The conversion uses an adaptive differential pulse code modulation (ADPCM) transcoding technique.

The Recommendation was prepared by ITU-T Study Group 15 and approved on 14 December 1990. It obsoletes G.721, which defined only the 32 kbit/s characteristics.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone calls are turned into numbers many times a second. This method squeezes those numbers so the sound takes about half the space, and the 32 in the name is how many thousand bits per second remain.

sections.title: The MIME Type Definition
sections.content:
The sub-type audio/32KADPCM holds binary audio data encoded in 32 kbit/s ADPCM exactly as defined by G.726. This is the same algorithm as in the deprecated G.721. No header information shall be included in the audio data, and the content transfer encoding is typically binary or base64.

For clarity the RFC adds one rule: little endian ordering of the four-bit code words. That is the default in ITU-T X.420 for the equivalent X.400 body part.

The type is a primary component of the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM). There, the Content-Description and Content-Disposition headers describe the audio body, and only little endian bit ordering is valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The audio is sent as a plain stream of sound numbers with no cover page. The only extra rule is about which half of each byte holds the first number.

sections.title: Packing Code Words into Bytes
sections.content:
The 4-bit code words MUST be packed into octets so that the first code word (A) goes in the four least significant bits of the first octet, and the second code word (B) in the four most significant bits. Later pairs are packed the same way into successive octets.

Encoders should preferably extend the sample with silence so there is an even number of code words. If a sample has an odd number of code words, the last code word shall be discarded.

Because implementations of G.726 may order the code words differently within a byte, a codec that supports the opposite ordering must reorder the code words before storing or retrieving this content type.
sections.plainLanguage: Each byte holds two small numbers like two eggs in a box. The first egg always goes in the right-hand slot. If there is one egg left over at the end, it is thrown away.

sections.title: IANA Registration Details
sections.content:
The registration template gives media type audio, sub-type 32KADPCM, no required and no optional parameters, and says binary or base64 is generally preferred. The published specification is ITU-T G.726 with little endian ordering. The listed applications are primarily voice messaging, the file extension is .726, the Macintosh file type code is APCM, and the intended usage is COMMON. The magic number entry is given as a question mark.

The authors are listed as the contacts and change controllers.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the form filled in to get the name officially written in the list of sound types.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says there are no known security risks with sending or playing raw audio data. Audio data is typically interpreted only by an audio codec, and any unintended information introduced into the data stream will result in noise.
sections.plainLanguage: Sound data is only played by a sound program, so stray bits just make crackling noise instead of causing harm.
